one_liner: Rust derive-based, protobuf-like binary encoding (a rewritten prost fork) that encodes and decodes faster than prost.
what_it_does: Bilrost is a schema-ful, tag-numbered binary format modeled on Protocol Buffers but deliberately not wire-compatible with it, plus its Rust implementation. You `#[derive(Message)]` on your existing structs; there is no .proto file or code generator. The API is prost-like (`encode`, `encode_to_vec`, `decode`), with extras: `prepend`/`encode_fast` for backward encoding, `decode_borrowed` for zero-copy `&str`/`&[u8]` fields, and opt-in distinguished (canonical) decoding.
how_it_is_fast: Nested length-prefixed data is written back to front into a rope-like `ReverseBuffer`, so each sub-message's length is known once its bytes exist. That gives single-pass encoding with no repeated length measurement (the README says prost re-measures nested messages). Varints are a 9-byte-max bijective LEB128 variant. Encoding has a 1-byte fast path, then a hard-coded binary search on length feeding a const-generic unrolled writer; decoding uses a fully unrolled slice decoder split into 32-bit pieces. Borrowed decoding skips string allocation, which the README calls often more than half of decode cost, and field order is enforced by tag deltas, so no duplicate or merge handling is needed.
when_to_use: Rust-only systems where you own both ends and want protobuf-style schema evolution (numbered fields, unknown fields skipped) without .proto files or generated types.
Deeply nested or many-field messages, where backward `prepend` encoding helps most: 2.4x faster than prost encode on log and mk48 in the shootout.
String-heavy payloads you can decode by borrowing: on log, bilrost's borrowed decode is 721 µs vs 2.12 ms owned (~2.9x). prost has no borrowed decoding in that table.
You need canonical bytes for hashing, signing or dedup: `#[bilrost(distinguished)]` reports or rejects non-canonical input.
no_std targets with an allocator (turn off the `std` feature; `hashbrown` feature for maps).
when_not_to_use: Anything that must talk protobuf (gRPC, other languages, existing .proto schemas). The wire format is incompatible, there is no schema DSL, only a Rust implementation exists, and there is no RPC support.

Throughput matters most and schema evolution does not: on the same log table bitcode (97 µs), savefile (155 µs) and nanoserde (191 µs) serialize 1.6-3.1x faster than bilrost's 300 µs prepend. postcard also decodes faster (1.74 vs 2.12 ms) and its output is smaller (725 KB vs 805 KB).
You need random access without decoding (zero-copy archives). Bilrost always decodes into structs; see rkyv.
You want JSON or text output from the same derive. It is not provided; the README says to use a separate tool such as serde.
Bus-factor concerns: one maintainer with no external backing (issue #5), 47 stars, pre-1.0 versioning with occasional API breaks (0.1016.0 raised the MSRV and removed hidden methods).

integration.dependencies: bytes (required); default features add bilrost-derive (syn 2/3, quote, proc-macro2, eyre, itertools) and thin-vec (detailed-errors); build-dep autocfg; optional arrayvec, bstr, bytestring, chrono, hashbrown, jiff, smallvec, smol_str, time, tinyvec for type support
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.68 (edition 2021; CI tests 1.68 and stable); `default-field-values` feature needs syn 3 and an unstable syntax
integration.platforms: Pure Rust, no_std + alloc capable. The self-copy prepend optimization turns on automatically only on x86_64. CI runs Ubuntu only; macOS and Windows jobs are commented out.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. No global state was seen; messages are your own structs, and ReverseBuffer is a plain owned Vec of boxed chunks, so both are Send/Sync when their contents are.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the API mirrors prost (derive Message, encode/decode into bytes::Buf/BufMut), but the wire format differs from protobuf and there is no .proto codegen, so it only replaces prost where you control every reader and writer

gotchas: Forward `encode` and backward `prepend`/`encode_fast` perform differently by workload: prepend is 1.9x faster than encode on mk48 but slightly slower on mesh. `encode_fast` returns a possibly non-contiguous ReverseBuffer; use `encode_contiguous`/`into_vec` when you need one slice.

Collections in messages default to `unpacked` (one field per element); long numeric arrays should use `packed`. Packed and unpacked are not interchangeable on the wire, and oneof variants require packed.

Distinguished decoding is opt-in and unsupported for floats and HashMap/HashSet (hash collections are not canonical). `u8`/`i8` and `Vec<u8>` byte strings need explicit `varint`/`plainbytes` encodings per the type table.

Decoding has a fixed recursion limit of 100 nesting levels (the `no-recursion-limit` feature removes it). The crate uses some `unsafe` in its buffers; the `forbid-unsafe` feature swaps in safe code at some cost in speed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: bitcode, savefile, nanoserde and postcard all beat bilrost on the same log table, so pick bilrost over them when you need tag-numbered, protobuf-style forward/backward compatibility or canonical decoding rather than peak speed. Choose minicbor (similar log serialize speed, slower mesh decode 9.43 vs 5.83 ms) only if you need a standard CBOR wire format.
verified_claims_summary: In rust_serialization_benchmark (run 2026-09-10; rustc 1.100.0-nightly with LLVM 23.1.1, fat LTO; AMD EPYC 9V74, 4 vCPUs), bilrost 0.1016.1 encoded the log dataset in 300 µs (prepend) and 397 µs (forward encode). prost 0.14.4's encode-only time was 731 µs, so bilrost was 2.4x and 1.8x faster. It decoded in 2.12 ms vs 2.68 ms (1.26x). prost's 1.89 ms populate+encode figure includes converting into prost-generated types, which bilrost avoids because it derives directly on the native structs; bilrost also leads prost on mesh, minecraft_savedata and mk48 (serialize 1.2-2.4x, deserialize 1.05-1.76x) with 8-18% smaller output.
status_note: Actively maintained by one author: last default-branch release commit 2026-08-14, 0.1016.1 published to crates.io 2026-08-27, about 148k downloads. Apache-2.0 and easy to adopt. Versioning is pre-1.0, but the author states the wire format is final and that it runs in production at Restate and Graft.
